To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the model of NASA's jet noise is valid for a wide range of Mach numbers and jet diameters, 2) the acoustic efficiency is independent of the rocket size and may be calculated with a simple formula, 3) the supersonic length is the adequate reference length and 4) a new model is proposed for a more accurate prediction of the acoustic environment at lift-off.

a jet noise model based on the NASA model of the 70s is able to reproduce the experimental data of a rocket exhaust jet in free space, and that the sound power peak is linked to the supersonic part of the flow, the latter being defined as the length of the flow for which the local Mach number equals 1.
the sound power peak of rocket freejets is located at about 1.5 times the supersonic length and that the acoustic efficiency of a freejet is independent of its size.

the following aspects: - a better understanding of the physical mechanisms of the freejet noise, - a model of the near sound field, - a model for the far sound field.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the jet noise model, as it is, is not suitable to simulate the acoustic environment of a launcher.
the jet noise model is able to reproduce with a good degree of accuracy the experimental data.
a model of the jet noise is now available, but its use requires a careful choice of its parameters and a precise knowledge of the jet exhaust conditions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the sound power peak of the near sound field is not dependent on rocket size, but on the supersonic length, for a given jet Mach number and nozzle exit pressure.
the acoustic efficiency of a rocket exhaust is a constant value for a given Mach and a given size, and that the sound field characteristics are related to the length of the supersonic jet.
the model is able to simulate the sound power level and its spatial characteristics, but that the sound pressure levels are over-estimated by about 3dB.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the jet noise model is a powerful tool, provided it is adapted to each application.
the jet noise model can be used to predict the noise level of a rocket exhaust, provided that the model is properly calibrated.
the acoustic efficiency of rocket exhaust is independent from the nozzle size and may be estimated with a simple semi-empirical relation.
